questions.text: We can state in one sentence which entrepreneurs we serve, which problem we solve for them, and what changes for them.
We have a written theory of change linking activities to outcomes, and we have revised it based on what we learned.
Our curriculum and support are adapted to the local sector and context rather than imported.
We design programme length, cohort size and support intensity deliberately for our entrepreneurs, and we know why.
We design programmes around entrepreneur demand, not only around what donors will fund.
We use written, published selection criteria and a scoring process that more than one reviewer applies.
We can show that we reach entrepreneurs who would not otherwise be supported, not only those already funded or well connected.
We record, for each applicant and each stage, who applied, who was selected and why, including rejected applicants.
Our cohort design lets entrepreneurs learn from vetted peers, and we track whether they do.
We have clear criteria and a process for graduating, exiting or pausing participants.
Our mentors and coaches are vetted, briefed and matched to each entrepreneur's needs, with local expertise where it matters.
We collect entrepreneur feedback on mentors and sessions and act on it.
Our services cover what entrepreneurs say they need most, including marketing, finance access and market linkages.
Core staff stay long enough to keep institutional knowledge, and we have a plan when someone leaves.
We use external consultants or partners for gaps in our own expertise instead of overpromising.
We have defined indicators with baselines for our entrepreneurs, such as revenue, jobs and finance accessed.
We track outcomes after the programme ends, not only during it.
We compare participants with a reasonable counterfactual, such as rejected or waitlisted applicants, or we are honest about the limits of attribution.
We track our programme costs and can state the cost per entrepreneur supported.
We use results findings in leadership decisions and report them, including negative results.
No single funder provides more than half of our income.
We hold at least some multi-year or core funding that is not tied to one project.
We earn some revenue from fees, services or success fees, and we know its share of our budget.
Our core mission is funded, and we are not mainly surviving on unrelated consulting work.
We hold a written financial plan and enough reserves to cover a funding gap.
We have a functioning board or advisory body that meets, with conflict-of-interest rules.
We are registered with Ghana's Data Protection Commission and handle entrepreneur data responsibly.
We have a written safeguarding policy, a complaints channel that entrepreneurs know about, and trained staff and mentors.
We hold up-to-date legal registration, tax filings and audited or reviewed accounts.
Donor reporting and contract obligations are tracked and met on time.
We make introductions to investors, buyers and partners, and track which ones led to deals.
Our investor and finance partners are active and suited to our entrepreneurs' stage, not only guests at pitch events.
We maintain an alumni network and contact alumni regularly.
We have working partnerships with other support organisations, government, banks or buyers, and we know what each partner does.
Market access support, the biggest reported barrier, is a deliberate part of our offer.
Women hold a meaningful share of selection decision roles and mentor panels.
We review our selection, curriculum and mentoring for bias against women, young people and local founders.
We reach rural entrepreneurs through design choices such as location, language and delivery, not only through open calls.
We set and report inclusion targets and break down results by gender, age and location.
We help entrepreneurs assess and respond to climate and environmental risks and opportunities.
